points.title: One owner word, then match the ending
points.rule: Mi is for one person or thing. Mis is for more than one. Tengo from day 4 says how many people you have. Es and son from day 3 say who they are. The adjective follows the noun and matches it: -o or -os for masculine, -a for feminine. Vivo and vive stay whole chunks today.

grammar.notYet: Su, nuestro, and tu. You may hear ¿dónde vive tu familia? Answer with mi and mis. The present-tense pattern for vivo and vive comes later.

phrases.spanish: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
phrases.english: I have a brother and a sister.

phrases.note: Se llama is the same idea as me llamo from day 1.
Learn vivo as a chunk. The vivir pattern comes later.

phrases.spanish: Mi abuela vive en la India.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.english: Yes, I have a sister. And you?

lines.speaker: Elena
lines.english: I have two brothers. There are three of us.

lines.speaker: Elena
lines.spanish: Mis padres viven en Sevilla. Yo vivo en Londres.
lines.english: My parents live in Seville. I live in London.

practice.title: Describe your people
practice.instruction: Talk about 3–4 people: names, where they live, what they do, and one quality. Use mi or mis, then es or son.
tips: Use ser for jobs and personality.
If you do not want to talk about family, describe friends instead.
